introduction.title: Probability essentials
introduction.short: Read a chance, an independence assumption and a complete-event trial.
introduction.goal: Read the first attendance model in plain language.
explain: Probability is a number from 0 to 1 describing chance under a model: an impossible event has probability 0 and a certain event has probability 1. A chance of 0.72 is 72 out of 100, or 72%. Across many comparable occasions, the attendance fraction should tend towards that chance under the model; exactly 72 of every 100 guests need not attend. Lesson 1 assumes this chance for teaching. It is not a measured attendance rate.

Independent attendance means that learning whether one guest attends does not change another guest’s chance in the model. Several guests can still attend together. Friends travelling together could break that assumption: knowing one is coming may tell you about the other. Independence is a modelling choice to check, not a property guaranteed by sending separate invitations.

For room overflow, one trial must contain the whole event, including every guest decision. Count attendees, then ask whether the count is greater than the seats. Exactly full still fits. A fraction is a part divided by a total: one overflow among four events is 1/4 = 0.25 = 25%. Below, 1 means attends and 0 means absent. Sum adds those guest decisions. These four hand-picked events illustrate counting; they are not random draws from the 72% model.
introduction.predict: With two seats, which of these four events overflows?
introduction.look: One guest decision and one whole-event overflow decision have different meanings. Only the event with all three guests overflows two seats. The printed 25% describes these four invented examples; it is not a simulation estimate of the first lesson’s room risk.
introduction.change: Change seats from 2 to 1. Predict which events now overflow, then run again. Keep the guest decisions unchanged.
introduction.question: Each of two guests has a 72% attendance chance. They travel together, so learning that one attends changes the other’s chance. What needs revisiting?
options: The independence assumption; the individual chances alone do not describe how they attend together.
The rule that exactly 72% of every small group must attend.
The idea that an overflow trial should contain the whole event.
introduction.feedback: Independence concerns the relationship between guest decisions. A shared journey can link them even when each person’s individual chance is unchanged. The guest chance is not the room-overflow probability, and a small group need not match its expected attendance fraction.
hints: Ask what knowing one guest’s decision tells you about the other.
Independent means that learning one decision does not change the modelled chance of the other.
introduction.limit: The events are deliberately invented to explain the counting rule. They are neither measured attendance nor a random simulation. Lesson 1 generates many possible events under an explicit probability model.
introduction.kind: Four invented events · a counting demonstration

lessons.title: Will the room be full?
lessons.short: Estimate the probability that attendance exceeds a room’s capacity.
lessons.goal: Estimate the probability that attendance exceeds a room’s capacity.
explain: An organiser has invited 150 people to a room with 110 seats. Suppose each guest has a 0.72 (72%) chance of attending. Assume independent attendance: learning one guest’s decision does not change another guest’s chance. This is an explicit teaching model, not a measured attendance rate. A simulation generates possible events under those assumptions.

One trial is one complete event: draw who attends, count them and compare the count with the seats. Repeating produces a distribution, the possible counts and how often they occur. A boolean is a True/False decision; NumPy counts True as 1 and False as 0. Averaging the overflow decisions therefore gives the fraction of whole events with attendance greater than 110.

NumPy is a Python library for array calculations. Its binomial generator counts yes/no successes among a fixed number of opportunities. Here those opportunities are the individual guests; one complete Monte Carlo trial is still the whole event. The arguments are invitation count, guest attendance chance and number of simulated events. The seed makes this particular run repeatable. Your estimate describes the model; checking whether its assumptions describe real guests is a separate task.
lessons.predict: Will raising the seat count change attendance, or only the overflow condition?
lessons.look: The comparison is strictly greater than the capacity. Exactly 110 guests fit in 110 seats. The boolean array contains one overflow decision per simulated event: True counts as 1 and False as 0, so its mean is the fraction of events that overflow.
lessons.change: Change seats to 120 while retaining the seed. Predict which outputs change.
lessons.question: You want the probability of at least 110 attendees. Which condition matches?
options: attendance >= 110
attendance > 110
attendance == 110
lessons.feedback: At least includes the boundary. Translating the question into the correct event is part of the model, before choosing a simulation count.
hints: Write the smallest count that qualifies.
Decide whether exactly 110 belongs in the event.
lessons.limit: Independent attendance with a known common probability is assumed. Shared weather or invitation groups could change the distribution.
lessons.notation: In the reference, X is attendance, c is the seat count, k counts overflow events and n counts complete simulated events. The hat on P marks an estimated probability.

lessons.title: What counts as one trial?
lessons.short: Identify the simulated unit and retain all outcomes belonging to it.
lessons.goal: Identify the simulated unit and retain all outcomes belonging to it.
explain: A trial contains one complete outcome for the question. A NumPy array stores values in a numbered arrangement and applies arithmetic to its entries. A two-dimensional array is a matrix: rows and columns. Here one row is one event and one column is one guest. Individual guests are ingredients, not separate observations of overflow.

Inspect the invented two-event example first: [[1,0,1],[0,1,0]]. Its shape (2,3) means two rows and three columns. Summing with axis=1 works across each row, giving attendance [2,1]. With axis=0 it works down the rows, giving guest-column totals [1,1,1]. Each 1 means attends; each 0 means absent. The code prints both calculations before generating more events.

A uniform random draw on [0,1) gives equally likely intervals of equal width: a draw below 0.6 occurs with chance 0.6. Comparing draws with that threshold gives boolean attendance decisions. Summarise each row before testing overflow. Averaging every cell instead estimates a guest attendance fraction. Later, x[:,0] selects every row of column 0; x[:3] selects the first three rows. Python starts numbering at zero.
lessons.predict: Does averaging individual guest decisions estimate the probability of an event overflowing?
lessons.look: Read the shape and axis before summarising. Array arithmetic acts entry by entry: counts > 5 makes one True/False decision per event. Six events provide very little precision for estimating overflow.
lessons.change: Change the random-draw shape `(6, 8)` to `(10000, 8)`. Keep the tiny invented example unchanged and each event’s guests together when calculating overflow.
lessons.question: For a five-task project, which object should one deadline trial contain?
options: One arbitrarily selected task.
All task durations needed to compute the project finish time.
Only tasks finishing late.
lessons.feedback: A project outcome requires its full set of task durations and scheduling rules. Task draws do not individually count as completed-project trials.
hints: Name the outcome the decision concerns.
List the inputs needed to calculate one such outcome.
lessons.limit: The rows and guest draws are independent in this model. Real events can share common influences.

lessons.title: Repeat the whole experiment
lessons.short: Build a repeated simulation without mixing inputs from different trials.
lessons.goal: Build a repeated simulation without mixing inputs from different trials.
explain: A Monte Carlo estimate averages a quantity calculated from random inputs. First define it for one complete trial, then repeat that rule. An indicator is 1 when a condition holds and 0 otherwise; averaging a loss indicator estimates the chance of a loss.

Here each event has attendance, ticket revenue and a fixed venue cost. Profit is revenue minus cost. NumPy applies the arithmetic entry by entry, keeping each count attached to its revenue. A sample mean adds all profits and divides by the number of events. Its target, expectation, is the average weighted by the model's outcome probabilities.

The code also reports percentiles: P10 and P90 are cutoffs with roughly 10% and 90% of outcomes at or below them. P50 is the median, the middle of the ordered outcomes. Finite-sample cutoffs may interpolate between values; the next lesson makes that visible. A positive expected profit can coexist with a substantial loss chance, so inspect both.
lessons.predict: Can an event have positive average profit and still lose money in some trials?
lessons.look: Expected profit and loss probability describe different aspects of the same trial distribution.
lessons.change: Raise the fixed cost by £100. Explain why every trial’s profit shifts by the same amount.
lessons.question: Two plans have the same mean profit. What else would inform a choice?
options: Nothing; equal means imply equal outcomes.
Only the largest simulated profit.
Loss probabilities, downside magnitudes and the decision maker’s objective.
lessons.feedback: Equal means can conceal different downside risks and trade-offs. State the decision objective before selecting a summary.
hints: Imagine one plan frequently makes a small gain and occasionally a large loss.
Inspect the distribution relevant to the decision.
lessons.limit: Ticket price and venue cost are fixed teaching assumptions. The model omits refunds, variable expenses and selection effects.
source: Art B. Owen · Monte Carlo theory, methods and examples
lessons.notation: In the illustration, $\Pi$ denotes profit, E means model expectation and P means probability. $P(\Pi<0)$ reads ‘the chance that profit is negative’.

lessons.title: See the outcomes before the headline
lessons.short: Read an outcome distribution and distinguish quantiles from a mean.
lessons.goal: Read an outcome distribution and distinguish quantiles from a mean.
explain: A histogram groups values into bins, intervals whose bar heights count observations. The ten delivery delays below are invented values in days. Most are small, with one large delay: a long right tail. We can learn to summarise that shape without first choosing a random-input distribution.

The mean is total delay divided by ten. The median, or P50, is the middle of the sorted values; here the fifth and sixth values are both 3 days. A quantile is a cutoff for a stated fraction. P90 means roughly 90% of outcomes are at or below the cutoff.

NumPy's default linear interpolation puts P90 one tenth of the way from the ninth value, 5, to the tenth, 15: 6 days. That cutoff need not be an observed delay. These percentiles describe the supplied outcomes, not uncertainty about an estimated mean. Keep the raw values beside the picture because changing bins can change its appearance.
lessons.predict: For a right-skewed distribution, must the mean equal the median?
lessons.look: The large delay lifts the mean above the median. The published P90 is 6 days by interpolation; nine of the ten supplied delays are at or below it.
lessons.change: Change the largest invented delay from 15 to 30 days. Predict what happens to the mean, median and P90, then run.
lessons.question: P90 delivery time is eight days. What does that describe?
options: A percentile of the modelled delivery-time outcomes.
A 90% confidence interval for the mean.
A guarantee that no delivery takes longer.
lessons.feedback: P90 is an outcome quantile. Some modelled deliveries exceed it, and the estimated quantile has its own numerical uncertainty.
hints: Name whether the quantity concerns outcomes or an estimated average.
Think about the upper 10% of outcomes.
lessons.limit: These ten delays are invented examples, not measured data or random draws. They illustrate summaries; they do not establish a delivery-delay model or a reliable future tail.
lessons.kind: Ten invented delivery delays · inspectable summaries

lessons.title: Reproduce a random run
lessons.short: Use seeds without confusing reproducibility with independent replication.
lessons.goal: Use seeds without confusing reproducibility with independent replication.
explain: A pseudo-random generator produces a deterministic sequence from an initial state. A seed makes that state reproducible. Record the generator, package version, seed and draw order when you need someone else to recreate a calculation.

Two generators initialised with the same seed produce the same sequence under the same implementation. They are useful for replaying an experiment, but are not independent replications. Changing the sequence of calls changes which draws enter each calculation.

A fresh seed can reveal numerical variation under the same model. It cannot reveal assumptions omitted from that model. For parallel work, independent child streams, separate pseudo-random sequences, provide a principled alternative to repeatedly reusing one seed; the reproducibility module returns to that design.
lessons.predict: Do two generators with the same seed provide two independent sets of evidence?
lessons.look: The replay establishes computational reproducibility for this procedure. It does not add another independent estimate.
lessons.change: Insert one extra random draw before generating b. Explain the resulting difference.
lessons.question: A colleague reruns your exact seeded simulation and obtains the same output. What was checked?
options: The model describes every possible real population.
The saved computational procedure was reproduced.
Two independent replications were collected.
lessons.feedback: The rerun checks the computation. Model validity and independent numerical replication require separate evidence.
hints: Ask what changed between the two runs.
Distinguish replaying a sequence from obtaining a new one.
lessons.limit: Identical seeds alone do not guarantee identical results across changed generators, package versions or draw ordering.

lessons.title: Check against an exact answer
lessons.short: Use a tractable case to challenge a simulation’s implementation.
lessons.goal: Use a tractable case to challenge a simulation’s implementation.
explain: When an exact answer is available, it is a valuable reference. Return to the room model: independent attendance with a fixed probability gives an exact binomial distribution for the attendance count.

A cumulative probability counts values at or below a threshold, P(X ≤ k). Its complement is the upper tail, the chance above k. SciPy's survival function sf(k) calculates that strict upper tail directly, matching attendance > seats. Direct tail calculation avoids loss of numerical accuracy when a very small answer is obtained by subtracting almost-equal numbers.

The simulation estimate will usually differ from the exact model probability because it uses finitely many trials. A discrepancy should be judged against Monte Carlo error, not an expectation of identical decimal strings. Agreement supports this implementation for this model, not the assumption that real attendance is independent.
lessons.predict: Should a finite simulation match the exact probability to every displayed decimal?
lessons.look: Both answers refer to the same model and boundary. A code error can hide if the supposedly independent reference repeats the same mistake.
lessons.change: Change both methods to the event attendance >= 110. Work out which survival-function argument is required.
lessons.question: Which exact expression matches $P(X\ge10)$ for integer X?
options: sf(9)
lessons.feedback: For an integer count, X >= 10 is the same event as X > 9. Boundary checks are a simple, useful verification tool.
hints: Write the allowed integer outcomes explicitly.
Find the largest excluded value.
lessons.limit: This checks a known binomial case. It does not validate every model built with the same random library.
lessons.notation: The model probability p is the exact reference; the estimate with a hat uses finitely many complete events. Run-to-run numerical error is the variation in that estimate over fresh simulations; lesson 15 quantifies it.

lessons.title: Sample weighted alternatives
lessons.short: Generate categorical choices with explicit probabilities.
lessons.goal: Generate categorical choices with explicit probabilities.
explain: Some inputs are categories rather than continuous measurements. A visitor might choose a standard, vegetarian or premium meal. Represent the categories and their probabilities together so their meaning stays inspectable. Mutually exclusive means one visitor cannot belong to two meal categories here; we also assume every visitor chooses one.

The probabilities must be nonnegative and sum to one. NumPy choice samples from the alternatives using those weights. The sample frequencies will fluctuate around the stated probabilities; they are not required to reproduce them exactly in one batch. Relative weights are different: [5,3,2] become [.5,.3,.2] by dividing by their total 10, but only if they really mean relative frequencies.

A category can select another calculation, such as ingredient cost. Averaging those costs estimates the expected cost under the assumed mix. This preserves the distinction between a category label and the numerical outcome it produces.
lessons.predict: Will a sample of ten meals necessarily contain exactly three vegetarian meals if their probability is 0.3?
lessons.look: The finite frequencies differ slightly from the input weights. The costs are a separate mapping from category to outcome.
lessons.change: Increase the premium weight and reduce the standard weight by the same amount. Predict the cost change.
lessons.question: Your category weights sum to 1.2. What should happen before simulation?
options: Check and correct their meaning and normalisation.
Interpret them as independent probabilities of exclusive categories.
Silently drop the least convenient category.
lessons.feedback: Exclusive category probabilities need a valid total. Normalising can be appropriate for relative weights, but that interpretation must be stated.
hints: Ask whether the alternatives are mutually exclusive.
Separate probabilities from arbitrary relative weights.
lessons.limit: The mix and prices are invented. Sampling a category does not establish that actual visitors follow these weights.

lessons.title: Count successes in a fixed group
lessons.short: Recognise when a binomial model fits a fixed set of independent opportunities.
lessons.goal: Recognise when a binomial model fits a fixed set of independent opportunities.
explain: A binomial count is the number of successes among a fixed number of independent opportunities, each with the same success probability. Its support is the integers from zero to the opportunity count.

The expected count is n times p. Variance is the model's average squared distance from that mean; standard deviation (SD) is its square root, back in count units. For this binomial model the variance is n times p times (1-p). Probability mass means the probability assigned to one possible integer count.

The example assumes thirty independent components each passing with probability 0.95. Compare sample summaries with the known model mean and variance. A sample variance estimates model variance from finitely many draws and uses ddof=1 to account for estimating their mean. Arbitrary time arrivals or group-linked outcomes need a different model.
lessons.predict: Can this model ever generate more successes than the number of opportunities?
lessons.look: The bounded integer support is part of the model. The sample variance uses `ddof=1` to estimate population variance from independent draws.
lessons.change: Replace `p=.95` with `p=.5`. Compare the spread as well as the mean.
lessons.question: Which setting directly violates this binomial model?
options: A fixed group of twenty independent attempts with common p.
A shared machine fault makes many attempts fail together.
A success probability between zero and one.
lessons.feedback: A shared fault induces dependence. A binomial model with independent attempts can then give misleading tail probabilities.
hints: Inspect what independent attempts means.
Ask whether one event changes many outcomes together.
lessons.limit: The model does not represent shared defects or varying pass probabilities without additional structure.
lessons.notation: X is the success count, n is the fixed opportunity count and p is the common success chance. The symbol ~ reads ‘is drawn from’ the named distribution.

lessons.title: Count arrivals in an interval
lessons.short: Use a Poisson model with an explicitly scaled observation interval.
lessons.goal: Use a Poisson model with an explicitly scaled observation interval.
explain: A Poisson count takes nonnegative integer values with no fixed upper limit. A homogeneous process has a constant event rate. Independent increments means counts in non-overlapping time intervals do not inform each other under the model; for example, the first half-hour's count does not change the next half-hour's distribution.

If the rate is four requests per hour, the expected count in half an hour is two. NumPy poisson takes that expected count, not a rate with unspecified units. Keep the duration conversion visible in the model.

Under this model the count variance equals its mean. Real observations with bursts, seasonality or shared causes may have more variation. Comparing empirical mean and variance is a useful diagnostic, although matching them would not prove the whole model.
lessons.predict: For a rate of four per hour, what mean belongs in a half-hour count generator?
lessons.look: The rate-times-duration product supplies the generator’s expected count. A larger interval changes the count distribution.
lessons.change: Change hours to 2. Retain the same hourly rate and compare zero-arrival probabilities.
lessons.question: A generator expects a mean count. You supply an hourly rate while modelling ten minutes. What is missing?
options: A random seed alone.
An extra fixed upper bound.
Conversion from rate to expected count over the specified duration.
lessons.feedback: The generator needs rate multiplied by duration in compatible units. A seed cannot fix a dimensional error.
hints: Write the rate’s units beside the duration.
Check that the product has units of events.
lessons.limit: A constant-rate Poisson model omits burstiness, periodicity and arrival dependence.
lessons.notation: $\lambda_{\rm window}$ is the expected number of arrivals in the chosen window; probability mass is the chance of each integer count.

lessons.title: Wait for the next event
lessons.short: Translate an event rate into the exponential waiting-time scale.
lessons.goal: Translate an event rate into the exponential waiting-time scale.
explain: An exponential waiting time is nonnegative and right-skewed. For a homogeneous Poisson process of rate lambda, the waiting time to the next event has mean one divided by lambda.

NumPy’s exponential generator takes that mean scale. Passing the rate directly would invert the intended behaviour: increasing a rate should shorten waits. Use compatible time units when taking the reciprocal.

The model is memoryless: conditional on having already waited, the remaining wait has the same distribution. This can be useful for simple arrival or failure models, but is unsuitable when ageing or scheduling changes the event hazard. The empirical conditional comparison below illustrates, rather than proves, that property. Hazard means the event rate conditional on still waiting; it stays constant in this exponential model.
lessons.predict: Should increasing the arrival rate make the average wait longer or shorter?
lessons.look: The two empirical means need not be identical. The conditional subset is smaller and has more sampling error.
lessons.change: Double the rate, then state the expected mean wait before running.
lessons.question: A scheduled bus is known to arrive every ten minutes. Is an exponential model automatically appropriate?
options: No; its memoryless random-arrival assumption needs justification.
Yes; every positive waiting time is exponential.
Yes; the mean determines every distribution.
lessons.feedback: Support and mean are insufficient to identify a waiting-time distribution. A schedule has structure that a memoryless model ignores.
hints: Consider whether already waiting tells you anything about the remaining wait.
Compare scheduled events with a constant random hazard.
lessons.limit: The example assumes a constant rate and independent increments; ageing and schedules need other models.
lessons.notation: T is waiting time, $\lambda$ is the event rate per time unit and E[T] is the model's mean wait.

lessons.title: Model symmetric variation
lessons.short: Check the support and spread of a normal input model.
lessons.goal: Check the support and spread of a normal input model.
explain: A normal distribution is a symmetric bell-shaped model, specified by mean μ and standard deviation σ. The notation N(μ,σ²) lists its mean and variance; NumPy's scale argument takes σ, not σ². Its possible values include every real number, including negatives.

The curve is a density: probability comes from area over an interval, not the height at one point. The whole area is one; a single exact value has zero probability in this continuous model. For zero-centred sensor errors, negative and positive values make sense. For a duration, negative values may make the model unsuitable.

The example adds sensor errors with SD 2 to a fixed reference. Clipping negative durations to zero would change their model by piling probability at exactly zero, a point mass. Check what the quantity can mean before selecting a familiar curve. Outcome SD describes individual errors; later MCSE describes numerical uncertainty in a summary.
lessons.predict: Will a normal distribution with a positive mean always generate positive values?
lessons.look: A familiar bell shape does not make a model suitable for every quantity. Check its support against the meaning of the input.
lessons.change: Increase the sensor-error standard deviation. Explain which uncertainty it changes.
lessons.question: You replace every negative normal duration with zero. What have you done?
options: Preserved the original normal model.
Created a different input distribution that needs its own justification.
Removed all model uncertainty.
lessons.feedback: Clipping changes the distribution, including adding probability at the boundary. A positive-support model may be a more appropriate starting point.
hints: Ask where the clipped probability goes.
Distinguish editing a distribution from observing better data.
lessons.limit: The sensor model assumes additive independent normal errors with no calibration bias.
lessons.notation: In this picture E is the sensor error, not the expectation operator. N(0,2²) has mean 0, variance 4 and SD 2.

lessons.title: Keep positive quantities positive
lessons.short: Interpret lognormal parameters on their underlying log scale.
lessons.goal: Interpret lognormal parameters on their underlying log scale.
explain: The exponential function exp(z), also written e to the power z, is positive. Here e is approximately 2.718. Its inverse is the natural logarithm log: exp(log(10))=10 and log(exp(2))=2. Logs turn multiplication into addition. A lognormal draw is exp(Z) for a normal draw Z, so it stays positive.

For lognormal X, log(X) has normal mean $\mu$ and SD $\sigma$. Its median is $e^\mu$ and its mean is $e^{\mu+\sigma^2/2}$. With log mean log(10) and log SD 0.7, the median is 10 while the mean is about 12.78. These are log-scale parameters, not the positive outcome's arithmetic mean and SD.

Multiplicative variation can support a lognormal model when the mechanism and evidence fit. Passing an average cost directly as the generator's mean usually gives a very different distribution: a desired median 10 needs log_mean=log(10). Increasing log_sd spreads the positive outcomes without changing that model median. The distribution has no finite upper bound.
lessons.predict: If the log-scale mean stays fixed and sigma increases, does the arithmetic mean stay fixed?
lessons.look: Positive support does not establish that a lognormal shape fits the domain. Compare its quantiles with evidence.
lessons.change: Set `log_sd` to 1.2 while keeping `log_mean` fixed. Compare median and mean.
lessons.question: Someone gives a median of 20 and a log-scale SD of 0.4. Which mean parameter belongs in the lognormal generator?
options: `np.log(20)`
lessons.feedback: For this parameterisation the log-scale mean is the logarithm of the median. The arithmetic mean of the positive variable is another quantity.
hints: Write the model median as $e^{\mu_{\log}}$.
Invert that relationship to obtain `log_mean`.
lessons.limit: A lognormal has no finite upper bound. Hard physical bounds or different tail behaviour require a different model.

lessons.title: Two different kinds of spread
lessons.short: Distinguish variation in outcomes from Monte Carlo error in an estimated mean.
lessons.goal: Distinguish variation in outcomes from Monte Carlo error in an estimated mean.
explain: Individual outcomes can remain highly variable even when their mean is estimated precisely. Outcome spread describes the simulated world. Monte Carlo error describes how much the numerical estimate changes when you rerun a finite simulation of that same world.

Generate many independent batches from one fixed input distribution. Each batch has its own sample mean. The standard deviation within a batch describes outcomes; the spread across batch means describes variation in the estimator.

Increasing the number of draws per batch usually reduces the latter under independent finite-variance sampling. It does not make the modelled outcomes more predictable, remove input uncertainty or establish that the distribution is a good description of reality. Name which uncertainty a reported interval addresses.
lessons.predict: Will more simulation trials make individual delivery times less variable?
lessons.look: Outcome SD stays near 20 while batch means become more concentrated. A single batch cannot reveal every source of model uncertainty.
lessons.change: Double the model’s outcome SD and repeat. Compare both kinds of spread.
lessons.question: A million runs give a very narrow interval for mean cost. What can still be large?
options: Only the random seed.
The spread of individual costs and uncertainty about the input model.
Nothing; every uncertainty has been removed.
lessons.feedback: Numerical precision is conditional on the model. Individual outcomes and the adequacy of the input assumptions remain separate questions.
hints: Name what is repeated when you add simulation runs.
Ask whether any new real-world observations were collected.
lessons.limit: The batches here are independent normal draws with finite variance. Other sampling schemes need different error calculations.
source: Art B. Owen · Monte Carlo theory, methods and examples
lessons.notation: $\bar X$ is a mean across n independent outcomes and σ is their model SD; its mean's SD is σ divided by sqrt(n).

lessons.title: Watch convergence without promising a winner
lessons.short: Recognise the typical square-root relationship between independent trial count and numerical error.
lessons.goal: Recognise the typical square-root relationship between independent trial count and numerical error.
explain: For independent identically distributed draws with finite variance, the sample mean approaches the model expectation as the sample grows. This law-of-large-numbers statement does not say that every additional draw moves the estimate closer to the answer. The abbreviation i.i.d. means independent and identically distributed. Identically distributed means every draw uses the same model. Finite variance means its average squared deviation has a finite value, the condition used by the error rule below.

The standard deviation of the sample mean is the outcome standard deviation divided by the square root of n. Four times as many draws therefore halves that standard deviation under the same model. It is a statement about repeated experiments, not a guarantee for one running trace.

Here the exact expectation of U squared for U uniform between zero and one is one third. The trace and repeated-batch error calculation let you inspect both convergence and its irregularity. Rare outcomes and heavy tails can make this simple picture difficult or invalid.
lessons.predict: Must the running estimate become closer to one third after every new draw?
lessons.look: The estimate can temporarily move away from the exact value. Error reduction is assessed across repetitions or with a justified error estimate.
lessons.change: Compare `n=100` and `n=10000`. Predict the typical error ratio before calculating it.
lessons.question: Under the independent finite-variance model, reducing standard error by a factor of ten generally needs what?
options: Ten times as many runs.
The same seed repeated ten times.
About one hundred times as many runs.
lessons.feedback: Standard error scales with one over the square root of n. A tenfold reduction therefore requires roughly a hundredfold count increase.
hints: Write SE proportional to $1/\sqrt n$.
Square the desired reduction factor.
lessons.limit: The square-root rule applies to this independent finite-variance estimator. It is not a universal rate for MCMC or quasi-Monte Carlo.
source: Art B. Owen · Monte Carlo theory, methods and examples
lessons.notation: $\overline{U^2}$ means average the squared uniform draws; n is their count. SE denotes the model standard deviation of that average across repeated runs.

lessons.title: Calculate Monte Carlo standard error
lessons.short: Estimate numerical uncertainty for a mean from independent simulation draws.
lessons.goal: Estimate numerical uncertainty for a mean from independent simulation draws.
explain: The Monte Carlo standard error, or MCSE, estimates the repeated-simulation standard deviation of an estimator. For a mean of independent identically distributed finite-variance outcomes, use their sample standard deviation divided by the square root of the number of trials.

The sample standard deviation uses `ddof=1` to account for estimating the mean. MCSE has the same units as the estimated mean. It is different from a relative error, which divides by an appropriate scale and becomes unstable near zero.

Repeated simulation batches provide an independent check of the formula in a tractable model. Compare the predicted standard error with the observed spread of batch means. This check relies on independent batches; replaying the same seed would make the apparent between-batch spread disappear.
lessons.predict: Should the MCSE have squared units or the same units as the outcome?
lessons.look: The estimated MCSE fluctuates because it uses a finite sample SD. It should be in the same broad range as the independent-batch and model calculations.
lessons.change: Replace `n=2000` with `n=8000`. Compare the observed change with the square-root prediction.
lessons.question: Your draws come from a slowly moving sequence of dependent draws. Can you automatically use $s/\sqrt{n}$ with the raw draw count?
options: No; dependence changes the variance of the estimator.
Yes; every array is independent by definition.
Yes; a seed removes dependence.
lessons.feedback: The ordinary formula assumes independent draws. Correlated chains require an autocorrelation-aware calculation, introduced in the advanced path.
hints: State the formula’s sampling assumption.
Ask whether a new draw depends on the previous one.
lessons.limit: A finite estimated MCSE can be misleading for poorly explored tails or infinite-variance outcomes.
source: Art B. Owen · Monte Carlo theory, methods and examples
lessons.notation: $Y_i$ is outcome i; $\bar Y$ is their sample mean. $\sum_i$ means add all the indexed outcomes. $s_Y$ is sample SD and n is the number of independent trials.

lessons.title: An interval for a simulated mean
lessons.short: Construct an approximate confidence interval for a model expectation.
lessons.goal: Construct an approximate confidence interval for a model expectation.
explain: An interval for an expectation describes numerical uncertainty about a fixed model mean, not the range of individual outcomes. Coverage refers to repeated independent simulations: if each run constructs a 95% confidence interval, about 95% should contain that same fixed mean when the method's assumptions hold. One interval can miss it.

For independent finite-variance draws whose sample mean is approximately normal, use mean ± critical value × MCSE. A two-sided 95% interval leaves 5% outside: 2.5% in each tail. The normal 97.5th percentile, stats.norm.ppf(.975), is about 1.96; symmetry supplies the lower endpoint.

The normal approximation can work for the mean of many skewed outcomes, but is not automatic for tiny samples or poorly explored tails. The exponential model has a known expectation to check. Compare the short interval for that expectation with the central 95% of individual waits. More draws narrow numerical error, not the underlying wait distribution.
lessons.predict: Should a 95% interval for the expectation contain 95% of the individual waits?
lessons.look: The interval and outcome percentiles target different quantities. The known expectation can miss an individual interval even when the procedure is working as intended.
lessons.change: Reduce the sample size to 20 and repeat across seeds. Explain why the approximation deserves more scrutiny.
lessons.question: A confidence interval for expected project duration is 9.9–10.1 days. What does it establish about individual projects?
options: They almost all last between 9.9 and 10.1 days.
It does not by itself describe the spread of individual project durations.
The deadline is guaranteed.
lessons.feedback: The interval targets the mean under the model. Deadline probabilities and outcome quantiles require separate calculations.
hints: Identify the interval’s target quantity.
Compare the mean with a randomly selected project duration.
lessons.limit: This normal interval is approximate and conditional on independent draws and adequate exploration of the outcome distribution.
lessons.notation: $\bar Y$ is the estimated mean, $s_Y$ is outcome sample SD and n is the independent draw count; ± means form a lower and an upper endpoint.

lessons.title: When zero failures is not zero risk
lessons.short: Report probability uncertainty without treating an unobserved event as impossible.
lessons.goal: Report probability uncertainty without treating an unobserved event as impossible.
explain: For independent yes/no trials, estimate event probability by event count divided by n. The plug-in standard error $\sqrt{\widehat p(1-\widehat p)/n}$ inserts that estimated fraction. With no observed failures it becomes zero, even though a rare model event may simply have been missed.

An exact binomial confidence interval uses binomial tails instead of this normal approximation. SciPy's `binomtest` returns a test record; call its `proportion_ci` method with `method="exact"` for a two-sided interval. Across repetitions, coverage is at least the stated level for independent trials with one common probability. Exact refers to that model calculation, not certainty about reality.

Two-sided 95% allocates 2.5% to each tail. A one-sided 95% upper bound allocates 5% to the lower-count tail: the probability of seeing zero failures at that upper probability is 0.05. With zero among n trials, solving (1-p)^n=0.05 gives upper bound 1−0.05^(1/n). The two conventions therefore have different upper limits.
lessons.predict: Can a finite run with zero failures rule out all positive failure probabilities?
lessons.look: The zero plug-in error estimate is not useful evidence of impossibility. The positive upper bounds quantify what the finite observation leaves unresolved under the binomial model.
lessons.change: Increase n to 10000 while retaining zero observed failures. Explain what evidence that larger n would require.
lessons.question: You simulate a rare event 100 times and never see it. What should you report?
options: The event is impossible.
Its probability is exactly zero to arbitrary precision.
The count, trial budget and an appropriate uncertainty bound under the model.
lessons.feedback: Zero observations are compatible with small positive event probabilities. A defensible report retains the count, denominator and method.
hints: Ask how often a rare event might be missed in a short run.
Use a probability interval that behaves sensibly at the boundary.
lessons.limit: Independent Bernoulli trials are assumed. The interval does not account for uncertainty in the failure model itself.

lessons.title: Plan a precision budget
lessons.short: Choose an independent-run budget for a stated numerical precision goal.
lessons.goal: Choose an independent-run budget for a stated numerical precision goal.
explain: Plan simulation count from the target and needed numerical precision. A Bernoulli outcome is one yes/no value, coded 1 or 0. Its variance p(1-p) is at most 0.25. That worst case gives a conservative planning count for the half-width h, the distance from an estimated probability to one endpoint of an approximate normal interval.

For two-sided 95%, z is about 1.96. Plan n by rounding z²×0.25/h² up to the next integer; ceiling means round up. In code half_width is h. Halving h needs about four times the draws. For a mean instead of a probability, replace 0.25 with a supplied outcome variance s².

Fix the count before examining the result, or use a sequential method built to support stopping. Repeatedly checking an ordinary fixed-count interval and stopping when a preferred conclusion appears changes the procedure. Keep numerical precision goals separate from the practical threshold of a decision.
lessons.predict: How does the planned count change if you halve the desired half-width?
lessons.look: The mean-planning count depends on an assumed or pilot SD. An unrepresentative pilot can make its precision forecast optimistic.
lessons.change: Try a probability half-width of .005. Explain the computational trade-off before increasing every example’s trial count.
lessons.question: Your first run is inconclusive for a useful threshold. Which continuation is defensible?
options: Report it, then use a prespecified new design or a valid sequential procedure.
Keep adding runs until the preferred option wins and hide the stopping rule.
Reuse identical seeded draws as extra independent evidence.
lessons.feedback: Additional computation can be useful, but its analysis should match the actual sampling and stopping procedure.
hints: Describe the whole procedure that produced the reported result.
Separate planning for precision from chasing a preferred conclusion.
lessons.limit: The formulas are approximate planning tools. They do not guarantee model validity, exact coverage or tail exploration.
source: Art B. Owen · Monte Carlo theory, methods and examples

lessons.title: An input needs a source
lessons.short: Attach units, provenance and uncertainty meaning to each model input.
lessons.goal: Attach units, provenance and uncertainty meaning to each model input.
explain: A numerical input can be a measured observation, an estimate fitted from data, or an explicit assumption. Those categories carry different evidence. A model that silently replaces an unknown value with a plausible constant hides a question the decision may depend on.

Keep a small input register before building a large simulation. Record the quantity, unit, value or distribution, source and conditions. A daily arrival rate cannot be combined with hourly service times without conversion. A fixed input still needs a reason to be treated as fixed.

The table below is an invented model register, not a dataset collected from a business. Its purpose is to make the distinction inspectable. The arithmetic converts a rate into a common time unit before later simulations combine demand with resources.
lessons.predict: Does writing an assumed rate in a table turn it into a measured fact?
lessons.look: Provenance remains a description of the evidence, not a property a calculation can verify for you.
lessons.change: Add an input for a service-time standard deviation and state what evidence would support it.
lessons.question: Which record is most useful for another person checking an input?
options: A number with no unit.
A value or distribution with units, source, conditions and uncertainty meaning.
A precise decimal count alone.
lessons.feedback: A reviewable input explains where it came from and what it means. Extra decimals cannot substitute for evidence.
hints: Ask what the next person would need to reproduce the choice.
Keep measurement conditions and units attached.
lessons.limit: The register makes assumptions visible; it does not establish that they are appropriate.

lessons.title: Sample the observations you have
lessons.short: Use empirical resampling while recognising what the sample cannot contain.
lessons.goal: Use empirical resampling while recognising what the sample cannot contain.
explain: An empirical distribution assigns probability to the observed values. Sampling those values with replacement is a simple way to propagate a recorded sample into a simulation without fitting a smooth distribution.

The example uses invented daily demand observations. They are assumed representative and exchangeable: each selected day can play the same role for the future question, so its position in the list is irrelevant. Sampling with replacement makes each selected value available again; one observation can appear several times.

The empirical model cannot draw beyond the observed range. Many resamples cannot establish that unobserved extremes are impossible. For seasonality or linked days, a different model may resample whole consecutive groups of days or account explicitly for day type. Those extensions need their own evidence.
lessons.predict: Can this empirical generator produce a demand larger than its largest input observation?
lessons.look: The support is inherited from the input sample. A precise simulated fraction is conditional on that empirical distribution.
lessons.change: Add an invented high-demand day of 150 and compare the decision-relevant tail probability.
lessons.question: You have observations only from quiet weekdays. What is the concern when forecasting weekends?
options: Resampling automatically creates weekend behaviour.
Increasing resample count repairs selection bias.
The empirical input may not represent the target days.
lessons.feedback: More draws reproduce the supplied empirical model more precisely. They do not add the missing weekend evidence.
hints: Identify which future conditions the observations represent.
Ask what sampling with replacement can and cannot invent.
lessons.limit: The input is invented. Independent daily resampling omits trends and dependence between days.

lessons.title: Fit a shape and inspect the fit
lessons.short: Fit a positive distribution and compare its quantiles with the input evidence.
lessons.goal: Fit a positive distribution and compare its quantiles with the input evidence.
explain: A fitted distribution estimates parameters from observations. It can interpolate between observed values and extrapolate beyond them, but its shape is another assumption. Parameter fitting does not establish that the distribution is suitable.

Fit a lognormal model to invented positive waits with loc=0. SciPy's shape is the SD of log(wait), and scale is exp(the mean of log(wait)); loc shifts the whole distribution. For NumPy's earlier generator this means SciPy shape=log_sd and scale=exp(log_mean). For example, log_mean=log(10) and log_sd=.7 correspond to shape=.7, loc=0, scale=10.

Compare empirical and fitted quantiles before using the fitted tail in a decision. A reasonably matching centre does not guarantee a matching tail. With a small sample, both fit assessment and parameter estimates are uncertain, so retain the observations and show sensitivity to plausible alternatives.
lessons.predict: Does a successful fit call establish that the fitted tail is realistic?
lessons.look: The fitted model makes predictions between and beyond observations. Those predictions need validation, not merely a converged optimiser.
lessons.change: Remove the largest observation as a separate sensitivity experiment, retain the original record and explain how the fitted upper quantile changes.
lessons.question: Two candidate models fit the middle of a small sample similarly but predict different extremes. What is useful?
options: Report tail sensitivity and seek evidence that distinguishes the models.
Choose whichever gives the cheapest decision and conceal the alternative.
Assume equal central fit proves equal tails.
lessons.feedback: Tail disagreement is a meaningful model uncertainty. It belongs in the report and can guide additional data collection.
hints: Identify which part of the distribution the decision uses.
Compare the candidate predictions in that region.
lessons.limit: Ten invented values are not sufficient to establish a reliable real-world tail. The fit also treats observations as independent.
lessons.notation: $\widehat\theta$ means fitted parameters; the hat marks an estimate from the finite observations.

lessons.title: Turn an expert estimate into a model
lessons.short: Translate a minimum, most likely value and maximum into an explicit bounded assumption.
lessons.goal: Translate a minimum, most likely value and maximum into an explicit bounded assumption.
explain: When data are sparse, people often provide a plausible minimum, most likely value and maximum. A triangular distribution is one transparent way to encode that particular shape assumption. Its bounded support and linear sides are choices, not consequences of asking an expert.

The mode is the peak of the density, not generally the median or mean. For a triangular model the mean is the sum of the three parameters divided by three. Hard bounds are strong claims: if the proposed maximum is merely a high percentile, treating it as an absolute bound excludes outcomes the expert may have intended to allow.

Treat the expert-supplied shape as a scenario and compare alternatives. Elicitation means asking for and recording those judgements; calibration means checking whether stated probabilities match relevant observed frequencies over repeated cases. Record what the minimum, peak and maximum mean, who supplied them and what evidence would change them.
lessons.predict: If the mode is 4 and the bounds are 2 and 12, must the mean be 4?
lessons.look: The hard upper bound guarantees no larger modelled duration. That guarantee comes from the assumption, not observations.
lessons.change: Compare `high=12` and `high=20` while retaining the same low and mode. Explain what changed in the input judgement.
lessons.question: An expert says “12 days is my 90th percentile”. Should you automatically use 12 as a triangular maximum?
options: Yes, percentiles and maximum bounds are interchangeable.
No; that would exclude the upper 10% they explicitly allow.
Only if you use many simulation runs.
lessons.feedback: A percentile and an absolute bound encode different claims. Clarify the elicited quantity before choosing a distribution.
hints: Ask what fraction of outcomes the expert allows above 12.
Compare that with a hard upper bound.
lessons.limit: The triangular form and hard bounds are illustrative elicitation choices. Other shapes can fit the same few judgements.

lessons.title: The parameters are estimates too
lessons.short: Separate uncertainty about an estimated parameter from variation in future outcomes.
lessons.goal: Separate uncertainty about an estimated parameter from variation in future outcomes.
explain: If a model parameter was estimated from a finite sample, treating it as known hides one source of uncertainty. A bootstrap can approximate uncertainty in a statistic by resampling independent observed units and recalculating that statistic.

Below each row is a bootstrap sample of invented independent demand days. Its mean is one bootstrap estimate of expected demand. Those means describe uncertainty in an estimated expectation under this resampling model. They are not a distribution of individual future daily demand. The percentile bootstrap interval takes the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of these recalculated means. It is an approximate interval for the expected demand, relying on representative independent days; small samples can give poor coverage.

For a predictive model, future outcome variation and parameter uncertainty can both matter, but they must be combined coherently. Simply adding their standard deviations or reusing the same variation twice does not create a justified model. Later Bayesian examples show another way to separate these layers.
lessons.predict: Will the bootstrap means have the same spread as individual daily demands?
lessons.look: The interval is an approximate percentile-bootstrap interval for an expectation. It inherits the sample’s representativeness and independence assumptions.
lessons.change: Repeat each observed day ten times in the input. Explain why treating those copied rows as fresh evidence would be misleading.
lessons.question: You bootstrap individual pupils although treatment was assigned to entire classrooms. What is missing?
options: A larger random seed.
A smoother histogram.
A resampling plan that respects classroom-level clustering and assignment.
lessons.feedback: Resampling must mimic the relevant independent units. Copying correlated rows into an independent bootstrap can understate uncertainty.
hints: Find which observations share an environment or assignment.
Preserve that dependence in a suitable resampling design.
lessons.limit: A bootstrap cannot recover unobserved populations or automatically repair correlated samples. Small-sample interval coverage can be poor.
lessons.notation: $d_i$ is original day i. A starred, barred d denotes the mean from one resampled set of days. In the question, classroom clustering means pupils in the same classroom can share dependence; the independent unit may be a whole classroom.

lessons.title: A scenario is not a probability
lessons.short: Compare conditional scenarios without inventing weights for them.
lessons.goal: Compare conditional scenarios without inventing weights for them.
explain: A scenario specifies a set of conditions to explore, such as ordinary, busy or disrupted demand. A probability distribution additionally assigns weights to possible values. Choosing scenario names does not supply those probabilities.

The simulation below estimates demand under three separate assumed arrival rates. Each row is conditional on that scenario. Reporting their average as an unconditional forecast would require a justified set of scenario weights and an explanation of what they represent.

Scenario analysis is useful even when weights are unavailable. It can identify which choices perform acceptably across plausible conditions and where a recommendation changes. State the scenario assumptions and keep conditional results separate from probabilistic claims about which scenario will occur.
lessons.predict: Do three named scenarios automatically have probability one third each?
lessons.look: Each probability refers to outcomes within a scenario. The table supplies no probability for which scenario occurs.
lessons.change: Add a fourth scenario and explain why that should not automatically reduce the probability assigned to the existing ones.
lessons.question: You have no evidence for scenario weights. What is a useful report?
options: Conditional results and the conditions under which the preferred decision changes.
An unexplained equally weighted average presented as a forecast.
A claim that scenario analysis is impossible.
lessons.feedback: Unweighted scenarios can reveal robustness and decision boundaries. They should remain conditional until weights are justified.
hints: Separate a condition being explored from a random variable with weights.
Ask which recommendation survives each condition.
lessons.limit: The three Poisson rates are authored scenarios. The code does not estimate their real-world probabilities.
source: Art B. Owen · Monte Carlo theory, methods and examples
lessons.notation: D is demand; here $\lambda$ is its expected count within the chosen time window. The vertical bar in $P(D>80\mid\lambda=40)$ reads ‘given the scenario with mean 40’.

lessons.title: Independence changes the answer
lessons.short: Compare a joint outcome under independent and dependent inputs.
lessons.goal: Compare a joint outcome under independent and dependent inputs.
explain: Independence means that learning one input does not change the distribution of the other. It is stronger than saying two inputs have different names or came from different spreadsheet columns. A marginal distribution is one variable's distribution considered on its own; matching the two marginals does not specify how they vary together.

Consider the sum of two positive costs. In the independent model each cost gets a separate uniform draw. In the shared model both costs move with the same draw. Their individual distributions are the same, but the distribution of their sum changes.

This distinction is important for budgets and deadline risks. Matching each input’s histogram does not determine the joint outcome. When relationships are uncertain, compare explicit dependency scenarios and identify which part of the decision they affect.
lessons.predict: If both costs become high together, should a high combined cost become more likely?
lessons.look: The expected totals are similar while the tails differ. Dependence can matter even when an average appears unchanged.
lessons.change: Compare the probability of a total below 50 as well as above 70.
lessons.question: Two models have identical input marginals. Must their total-cost tails match?
options: Yes, the marginals determine every sum distribution.
No, the dependence structure also matters.
Only the number of simulation runs matters.
lessons.feedback: A joint model requires marginal behaviour and dependence. Equal individual histograms can produce different combined risks.
hints: Ask whether large inputs can occur together.
Compare a shared draw with separate draws.
lessons.limit: Perfectly shared draws are a deliberate stress case, not an estimate of actual dependence.
source: Art B. Owen · Monte Carlo theory, methods and examples

lessons.title: Make the shared cause visible
lessons.short: Represent common conditions once per trial and propagate them to related inputs.
lessons.goal: Represent common conditions once per trial and propagate them to related inputs.
explain: A common cause is a simulated condition that influences several outcomes. It should be drawn once for the relevant unit. Drawing a fresh weather condition for every calculation in one event would erase the relationship the model intends to represent.

Here a busy-day factor affects both arrival counts and average spending. Each trial draws one factor and passes it into both calculations. Conditional on that factor, additional randomness can still remain in each outcome.

This hierarchical model draws a shared condition first, then outcomes given that condition. The factor is latent, meaning unobserved in the scenario, rather than a separate measured input. It is one possible mechanism, not proof about a real shop. Inspect intermediate values and challenge the shared-cause assumption.
lessons.predict: What happens to the intended dependence if you redraw the day factor separately for spending?
lessons.look: The model makes the common factor inspectable. Revenue inherits both its direct and indirect effects.
lessons.change: Use an independently redrawn factor for spending as a separate model, then compare the revenue distribution.
lessons.question: A regional storm affects several deliveries. Where should its state be drawn?
options: Independently for every line of arithmetic.
Only after observing whether a shipment was late.
Once per relevant regional-time trial, then shared by affected deliveries.
lessons.feedback: The draw should represent the common event at its intended scope. Reusing it within that trial preserves the modelled shared influence.
hints: Name the unit to which the storm belongs.
Keep all outcomes from that unit attached to the same state.
lessons.limit: The busy-day mechanism is invented, and the chosen spending noise is not fitted to observations.
source: Art B. Owen · Monte Carlo theory, methods and examples
lessons.notation: F is the shared busy-day multiplier; log(F) is normal with mean 0 and SD .25. The arrows mean use that same F in both calculations.

lessons.title: Correlation does not tell the whole story
lessons.short: Recognise dependence that a near-zero linear correlation can conceal.
lessons.goal: Recognise dependence that a near-zero linear correlation can conceal.
explain: Pearson correlation measures how strongly two quantities vary along a straight-line relationship. It ranges from -1 to 1: +1 is a perfect increasing line, -1 a perfect decreasing line, and zero means this linear summary finds no association. Zero need not mean independence.

Generate a symmetric input X and set Y to its absolute value, written |X|: remove the sign, so |-2|=2. Knowing X determines Y, yet positive and negative linear contributions cancel and correlation can be near zero. The V-shaped plot reveals what the coefficient misses.

This is also a reminder that an observed correlation does not identify a causal mechanism. In a simulation the relationship is known because the generator defines it. In measured data, shared causes, selection and direction need separate reasoning. Use a dependency model that reflects the mechanism relevant to the question.
lessons.predict: Can one variable determine another while their Pearson correlation is near zero?
lessons.look: The coefficient hides the V-shaped relationship. A single correlation number is not a complete joint distribution.
lessons.change: Replace Y with X plus small noise and compare the scatterplot and coefficient.
lessons.question: A measured correlation is zero. Which conclusion is justified without additional assumptions?
options: There is no detected linear association in that summary; nonlinear dependence may remain.
The variables are independent.
Changing one cannot affect the other.
lessons.feedback: Zero Pearson correlation concerns a linear summary. Independence and causal effects are stronger claims.
hints: Think about the shape in the plot.
Ask what information the coefficient discards.
lessons.limit: The example defines exact nonlinear dependence. It does not provide a general method for discovering causal structure from observations.

lessons.title: Generate correlated normal inputs
lessons.short: Construct a multivariate normal draw with an explicit covariance matrix.
lessons.goal: Generate two correlated normal inputs using shared and independent variation.
explain: Start with independent standard normal draws $Z_1$ and $Z_2$: each has mean 0 and SD 1. Choose correlation ρ between -1 and 1. Set $A=Z_1$ and $B=\rho Z_1+\sqrt{1-\rho^2}Z_2$. The second input shares part of A and adds fresh independent variation; the coefficients preserve its model variance.

For ρ=.7, the shared coefficient is .7 and the fresh coefficient is $\sqrt{.51}$, about .714. B's variance is $.49+.51=1$, while its correlation with A is .7. Covariance is the expected product of deviations from the means; a positive value indicates movement in the same direction. For these standardised variables, covariance equals correlation.

Scale and shift into units: cost A is $100+10A$ and cost B is $80+8B$. Standardised means zero mean and unit SD; scaling changes covariance and units but preserves correlation here. The printed covariance matrix is a table: variances down the diagonal and pairwise covariances off it. Nonlinear transformations can change correlation, so check the resulting joint model.
lessons.predict: If correlation changes from .7 to −.7, must either input’s own variance change?
lessons.look: Check mean approximately 0, variance approximately 1 and covariance approximately ρ before scaling. The finite sample approximates those model quantities; it need not match exactly.
lessons.change: Try correlations 0 and -0.7. Compare total-cost spread while keeping the marginals fixed.
lessons.question: You specify a correlation of 1.4 between standardised variables. What should you do?
options: Increase the sample count to make it valid.
Reject or revise the invalid dependence specification.
Clip the generated results after simulation.
lessons.feedback: Correlation must lie between -1 and 1. Outside that range, sqrt(1−rho²) is not real. Revise the invalid dependence specification before generating draws.
hints: Check the mathematical constraints on correlation.
Check the coefficients that keep the second input’s variance equal to one.
lessons.limit: Normal inputs allow negative values and linear dependence. They may be inappropriate for bounded or strongly skewed quantities.
lessons.notation: $\rho$ is the requested correlation; $Z_1,Z_2$ are independent mean-zero, unit-SD normal draws. The square-root coefficient keeps B's variance equal to one. The `assert` line stops with a message if the chosen correlation is invalid.

lessons.title: Sample one condition after another
lessons.short: Use conditional sampling to preserve relationships and constraints.
lessons.goal: Use conditional sampling to preserve relationships and constraints.
explain: Conditional sampling specifies a distribution after a relevant condition has been drawn. It gives a transparent sequence: simulate the state, select the appropriate input model, then simulate the outcome from that model.

In this event example, rain is drawn once per event. Attendance probability is lower on rainy days. The guest count is then drawn using the event’s probability. Marginally, guests share a weather influence, so the resulting attendance distribution is not the same as one fixed-probability binomial in every respect.

The law of total expectation gives a useful exact mean check: average the conditional expectations using the state probabilities. Matching that mean does not establish the correct tail shape. Compare both the overall distribution and the conditional groups when checking a model.
lessons.predict: Can replacing the two weather-dependent probabilities with their average preserve the mean while changing the spread?
lessons.look: The two conditional groups have different centres. The mixed distribution includes between-weather variation.
lessons.change: Compare against a fixed-probability binomial with `p=.71`. Inspect its variance and overflow probability.
lessons.question: A delivery duration depends on its route. Which generation order preserves that model?
options: Draw duration first, then assign a convenient route afterwards.
Always use one overall mean duration.
Draw a route, then draw duration from that route’s stated conditional distribution.
lessons.feedback: The route selects the conditional model. Drawing independent durations and labels would generally erase the intended relationship.
hints: Identify which condition chooses the distribution.
Preserve that condition within the same trial.
lessons.limit: The rain probabilities are assumptions, and weather effects are simplified to two event states.
lessons.notation: $X\mid p$ reads ‘attendance X given guest chance p’. The weather selects p once for each complete event.

lessons.title: Stress-test the dependency assumption
lessons.short: Report how a decision changes across plausible dependence structures.
lessons.goal: Report how a decision changes across plausible dependence structures.
explain: Sometimes you have credible marginal input distributions but weak evidence for dependence. Treating one convenient correlation as known can conceal a decision-sensitive assumption.

Compare a range of correlations while holding both standardised marginal distributions fixed. Each row below is a separate dependency scenario. The probability of a combined high cost can change because the two costs become high together more often.

Do not average the rows into one forecast without a justified model for the correlation uncertainty. Instead identify whether the recommendation changes across the range, what evidence would distinguish the scenarios, and whether a conservative action is affordable. This is a sensitivity analysis of a relationship, not a proof that any particular correlation is correct.
lessons.predict: Which changes more directly with positive dependence here: the marginal means or the chance of a large sum?
lessons.look: Reusing the base normal draws makes scenarios easier to compare. It does not assign probabilities to the scenarios.
lessons.change: Choose a decision rule such as $P(\mathrm{total}>205)$ below .05. Identify which dependence scenarios meet it.
lessons.question: A recommendation reverses under two plausible correlation assumptions. What should you report?
options: The dependency sensitivity and the evidence needed to resolve it.
Only the more favourable assumption.
That a very large simulation count makes the reversal disappear.
lessons.feedback: The uncertainty is in the model specification. More trials reduce numerical noise within each scenario but do not select the right scenario.
hints: Separate a model change from a seed change.
Ask whether the practical choice depends on that assumption.
lessons.limit: These normal-cost scenarios are illustrative and share base draws. Their joint variation is not evidence about actual cost correlation.
source: Art B. Owen · Monte Carlo theory, methods and examples
lessons.notation: μ and σ name each input's mean and SD. ρ names the assumed correlation; the scenario values have not been assigned probabilities.

lessons.title: Will the project finish on time?
lessons.short: Propagate uncertain task durations into a project deadline probability.
lessons.goal: Propagate uncertain task durations into a project deadline probability.
explain: A project estimate needs a rule for combining task durations. Start with three tasks that must run in sequence, so the project finishes when their durations have been added. The scheduling assumption is part of the model.

Each task uses an invented triangular distribution with a minimum, mode and hard maximum. One trial draws all three task durations and adds them. A deadline probability counts how many trial totals meet the specified boundary.

Report a central duration and an upper quantile alongside the deadline probability. Those summaries answer different planning questions. This first model assumes independent durations and no shared staffing or rework; later lessons introduce dependencies and parallel work rather than hiding them in an arbitrary extra margin.
lessons.predict: Does adding the three most likely durations give the most likely project duration automatically?
lessons.look: The sum’s distribution comes from the full task distributions. A sum of modes is not generally the mode or a chosen quantile of the sum.
lessons.change: Make the second task’s maximum 16 days. Explain the change in deadline risk.
lessons.question: Two tasks must run one after the other. Which trial calculation matches?
options: The maximum of their durations.
The sum of their durations.
Their smaller duration.
lessons.feedback: Sequential tasks add. A maximum applies to parallel branches that must both finish before the next stage.
hints: Draw the order in which work can occur.
Ask whether one task can start before the other finishes.
lessons.limit: All task distributions and hard bounds are assumptions. The model omits rework, resource conflicts and common causes.

lessons.title: How much contingency is enough?
lessons.short: Choose a budget reserve using an explicit target and cost distribution.
lessons.goal: Choose a budget reserve using an explicit target and cost distribution.
explain: A contingency reserve is meaningful only relative to a baseline budget and a target outcome. A reserve chosen to cover 90% of modelled costs differs from a reserve based on expected cost or the largest trial observed.

This example combines uncertain labour hours, a fixed hourly rate and an uncertain materials quote. The quantities and prices are invented. One trial must retain its own labour and materials draws before the costs are added.

P90 total cost minus the stated baseline gives the additional amount needed for a 90% modelled cost threshold, floored at zero if the baseline already exceeds P90. This is an outcome quantile, not a confidence interval. Its numerical precision and the credibility of the cost assumptions still need checking.
lessons.predict: Is the maximum observed cost a stable definition of a 90% contingency reserve?
lessons.look: The baseline and chosen coverage target are decision inputs. Different targets legitimately produce different reserves.
lessons.change: Compare reserves for P80, P90 and P95 while retaining the same trial costs.
lessons.question: A reserve is said to “cover uncertainty”. What specification is still needed?
options: Only the model’s seed.
A histogram colour.
The baseline, cost boundary, coverage target and assumptions.
lessons.feedback: A useful reserve statement names what spending it covers and the outcome target. It is conditional on the cost model.
hints: Ask what counts as total cost.
State the baseline and tolerated overrun probability.
lessons.limit: This teaching model omits dependencies, inflation and changes in scope. No actual budget has been estimated.
source: Art B. Owen · Monte Carlo theory, methods and examples

lessons.title: Enough food without too much waste
lessons.short: Compare shortage and waste under the same simulated attendance outcomes.
lessons.goal: Compare shortage and waste under the same simulated attendance outcomes.
explain: Catering is a decision problem because both preparing too little and preparing too much have consequences. A demand forecast alone cannot choose a food quantity without an objective or service constraint.

Use the same simulated attendance for every preparation option. Each trial has a shortage count and a waste count. Weighting them by stated penalties gives a loss measured in a common unit. Those penalties are decision assumptions, not properties of the random generator. For one event, shortage is attendance above the prepared meals, floored at zero. Waste reverses that difference; neither count can be negative.

The lowest expected loss can differ from the option with the smallest shortage probability. Report both if service quality matters. Reusing the same events for all options makes their comparison more precise without asserting that the events are real observations.
lessons.predict: Will the preparation quantity with the lowest shortage probability necessarily minimise expected loss?
lessons.look: The attendance draws stay identical across options. Only the policy and the resulting loss calculation change.
lessons.change: Increase the shortage penalty from 12 to 30 and compare the ranking.
lessons.question: Why compare all preparation options using the same attendance draws?
options: It isolates option differences under matched simulated conditions.
It guarantees the model describes actual guests.
It makes the options’ costs identical.
lessons.feedback: Shared simulated conditions support a cleaner paired comparison. They do not validate the attendance or penalty assumptions.
hints: Separate variation in demand from variation caused by changing an option.
Compare both options within one possible event.
lessons.limit: Shortage and waste penalties are invented. Dietary constraints, food safety and logistics are outside this model.
source: Art B. Owen · Monte Carlo theory, methods and examples
lessons.notation: $(x)_+$ means max(x,0), the positive part. $A_i$ is attendance in event i, m is prepared meals, and L is the resulting penalty in pounds.

lessons.title: How uncertain is a calculated measurement?
lessons.short: Propagate input measurement distributions through a nonlinear calculation.
lessons.goal: Propagate input measurement distributions through a nonlinear calculation.
explain: A calculated quantity can be uncertain because its measured inputs are imprecise. Monte Carlo propagation draws plausible input values under a measurement model and recalculates the derived quantity for each trial.

For a rectangle, area is width times height. The supplied normal distributions represent uncertainty about the dimensions given the stated measurements, not a collection of new panels. Calibration compares an instrument with a reference and may reveal a shared offset. Such a shared uncertainty must be modelled jointly; independent repeated-reading noise is a different interpretation.

The resulting area distribution is an output of the joint input model. Its percentiles describe propagated measurement uncertainty under those assumptions. Dividing their spread by the square root of the simulation count would instead address numerical error in an estimated summary, not make the panel’s dimensions more certain.
lessons.predict: Does running more area calculations improve the physical measuring instrument?
lessons.look: The specification fraction depends on the interpretation and calibration of the input distributions. It is not a universal confidence statement.
lessons.change: Introduce a shared calibration offset to width and height in a separate model. Explain what additional evidence that offset needs.
lessons.question: What mainly reduces propagated physical measurement uncertainty?
options: Repeating the same simulation indefinitely.
Better measurement evidence or a justified improved measurement model.
Printing more decimal places.
lessons.feedback: More trials improve numerical precision. Reducing uncertainty about dimensions requires new evidence or better justified modelling.
hints: Name whether the uncertainty comes from the instrument or finite computation.
Ask what new information the change supplies.
lessons.limit: The independent normal input distributions are teaching assumptions, not a calibrated metrology analysis.
source: Art B. Owen · Monte Carlo theory, methods and examples
lessons.notation: W is width, H is height and A=WH is area; centimetres times centimetres gives square centimetres.

lessons.title: How reliable is a whole product?
lessons.short: Translate a component relationship into a system success event.
lessons.goal: Translate a component relationship into a system success event.
