explain: A Markov chain generates its next state from its current state. Metropolis proposes a move, then accepts or keeps the current value. A symmetric proposal has equal forward and reverse move densities: normal steps centred on the current value have this property. Its acceptance chance is the candidate target density divided by the current target density, capped at one.

Stationarity means a whole target distribution is unchanged by one transition when the current state already has that distribution. A valid acceptance rule preserves it; this does not prove approach to it from an arbitrary starting value, called convergence. Use log densities to avoid tiny ratios. Reject out-of-domain proposals; clipping them would change the proposal rule.

Keep rejected states as repeated values: they are part of the chain. Warm-up is an initial segment set aside to reduce dependence on the chosen start; some algorithms also tune during it. Here its fixed length is a teaching convention, not proof of convergence. Compare the retained mean with the known beta reference and inspect movement, not acceptance fraction alone.
lessons.predict: Should a rejected proposal disappear from the recorded chain?
lessons.look: The trace is a diagnostic view, not a convergence certificate. Repeated states are an essential part of the sampler.
lessons.change: Compare proposal scales .005 and .8. Observe movement as well as the acceptance fraction.
lessons.question: A tiny proposal has a high acceptance fraction but hardly moves. What does this suggest?
options: High acceptance alone does not establish efficient exploration.
All accepted values are independent.
The posterior must be very narrow.
lessons.feedback: Small steps can produce strong serial dependence. Assess exploration and numerical error rather than maximising acceptance alone.
hints: Look at distance moved per iteration.
A long sequence of nearby states may provide little new information.
lessons.limit: One chain and one trace cannot rule out nonconvergence. This unimodal benchmark is intentionally easier than many posterior targets.
source: Art B. Owen · Monte Carlo theory, methods and examples
lessons.notation: Current x and proposed y are candidate values of the unknown probability p. The target is beta(20,14); the normal proposal supplies a step from x, not a new independent posterior draw.

lessons.title: Correct an asymmetric proposal
lessons.short: Include the reverse-to-forward proposal ratio in Metropolis–Hastings.
lessons.goal: Include the reverse-to-forward proposal ratio in Metropolis–Hastings.
explain: Let x be current and y proposed. $q(y\mid x)$ is the density of proposing y from x; $q(x\mid y)$ is the reverse density. For target density π, Metropolis–Hastings uses target ratio π(y)/π(x) times reverse/forward proposal density, capped at one. In a symmetric walk those proposal densities cancel.

An independence proposal draws from fixed q regardless of x. Then the forward density is q(y) and reverse density q(x); they can differ even though the draw does not depend on x. Omitting the correction generally changes the stationary distribution, the distribution preserved by a transition. Here proposal beta(3,3) is corrected back to target beta(20,14).

Retain rejections and set aside a starting segment as before. Irreducibility means the transition can reach relevant target regions, possibly over several steps; a density ratio cannot repair an unreachable region. One matching mean is an implementation check, not proof that the sampler explored the whole target.
lessons.predict: Does drawing an independence proposal make the proposal-density correction unnecessary?
lessons.look: The proposal correction uses current over proposed density for an independence sampler. Reversing that ratio implements a different algorithm.
lessons.change: Change the proposal to beta(10,10) in both the draw and `log_q`. Inspect acceptance and multiple seeds.
lessons.question: For q(y|x), what proposal factor belongs in the acceptance ratio?
options: q(y|x) / q(x|y).
q(x|y) / q(y|x).
No proposal factor for any algorithm.
lessons.feedback: The reverse-to-forward factor balances the proposed probability flows when forward and reverse moves have different proposal densities.
hints: Identify the proposed forward move x to y.
The correction is reverse density divided by forward density.
lessons.limit: Support and irreducibility still matter. A density ratio cannot rescue a proposal that never reaches relevant target regions.
source: Art B. Owen · Monte Carlo theory, methods and examples
lessons.notation: The vertical bar reads ‘given’. Here $\pi$ is target density, not the circle constant; q is proposal density. An independence proposal uses q(x)/q(y) as its reverse/forward factor.

lessons.title: Update one conditional at a time
lessons.short: Implement a Gibbs sampler using the latest value of each coordinate.
lessons.goal: Implement a Gibbs sampler using the latest value of each coordinate.
explain: Gibbs sampling updates components by drawing from their conditional distributions given the other components. Exact conditional draws require no Metropolis rejection step. The resulting sequence is still a Markov chain and its successive states are usually dependent.

For a zero-mean bivariate normal with unit marginal variances and correlation rho, X given $Y=y$ is normal with mean $\rho y$ and variance 1-rho squared. The conditional for Y is analogous. First update X from the current Y, then update Y from the newly drawn X.

The code records a state after both coordinate updates, called a sweep here. Strong correlation can slow movement along a narrow joint distribution even though every conditional draw is accepted. The known means and covariance supply checks; they do not make correlated draws independent. Lag-one correlation compares neighbouring retained states: the recorded sequence with a copy shifted by one row. A large value warns that rows supply less independent information.
lessons.predict: In the second update of a sweep, should Y condition on the old X or the newly drawn X?
lessons.look: Conditioning uses the latest state. The lag correlation warns against treating the kept row count as an independent sample count.
lessons.change: Increase rho to .98. Keep enough iterations to inspect the much slower movement.
lessons.question: Every Gibbs update is accepted. What can still make the sampler inefficient?
options: Serial dependence caused by the target geometry.
An obligatory acceptance correction for these exact conditional draws.
The absence of a random seed.
lessons.feedback: Acceptance is not the same as independent information. Strong conditional dependence can make exploration slow.
hints: Inspect the lag correlation.
Compare how quickly coordinates move across the full target range.
lessons.limit: These exact normal conditionals are tractable. More complex targets may need other conditional samplers and stronger diagnostics.
source: Art B. Owen · Monte Carlo theory, methods and examples

lessons.title: Account for serial dependence
lessons.short: Estimate a mean-specific effective sample size rather than using the independent-draw SE.
lessons.goal: Estimate a mean-specific effective sample size rather than using the independent-draw SE.
explain: Autocorrelation compares a sequence with itself shifted by a lag: lag 1 pairs neighbours, lag 2 pairs values two steps apart. Stationarity means their joint distribution does not change with the position in the sequence. For a stationary sequence with finite variance and sufficiently decaying correlations, the mean's variance includes these lag contributions.

The correlation-time factor τ is 1+2×(lag-1 correlation+lag-2 correlation+…). Count only positive lags; their correlation values can have either sign. If the correlations are .5, .25, .125,…, they sum to 1, so τ=3: N rows provide about N/3 independent-draw equivalents for this mean. Mean ESS≈N/τ and mean SE≈outcome SD/sqrt(ESS). A tail indicator can have a different ESS.

Use the supplied AR(1), a first-order autoregression: next=ρ×previous+fresh normal noise with SD sqrt(1−ρ²). The initial standard normal draw makes this toy sequence stationary. At ρ=.9, the exact correlation sum gives τ=(1+ρ)/(1−ρ)=19 and large-sample ESS≈N/19. The code calculates sample lag correlations directly, adding successive pairs until a nonpositive pair or the stated lag cap; the cutoff is an approximation, not a convergence test.
lessons.predict: For positively correlated draws, will the iid formula usually overstate or understate mean precision?
lessons.look: The known AR(1) approximation gives a reference for this experiment. ESS is not a guarantee that an arbitrary MCMC chain reached its target.
lessons.change: Compare `rho=.3` and `rho=.95`. Repeat with independent seeds and inspect ESS variability.
lessons.question: Can a large ESS for the parameter mean guarantee an accurate rare-tail probability?
options: Yes, all statistics share one ESS.
No; dependence and error are statistic-specific, and target exploration also matters.
Yes, if the chain has more than 1000 rows.
lessons.feedback: Different functions of a chain have different dependence. Tail accuracy requires its own assessment alongside convergence checks.
hints: Replace the parameter by a threshold indicator.
Ask whether that new series has the same autocorrelation.
lessons.limit: This simplified calculation is for positively correlated, stationary AR(1) draws with finite variance. The lag cap can miss long dependence and τ is floored at 1. Negative correlations can legitimately give ESS greater than N, so this is not a general ESS routine. It does not diagnose warm-up, missed modes or tail accuracy.
source: Vehtari et al. · Improved R-hat and MCMC diagnostics
lessons.notation: $\tau$ is the mean's correlation-time factor, N is retained row count, s is sample outcome SD and ESS is the independent-draw equivalent for this specific mean.

lessons.title: Compare multiple chains
lessons.short: Compute rank-normalised and folded split R-hat and explain its diagnostic limits.
lessons.goal: Compute rank-normalised and folded split R-hat and explain its diagnostic limits.
explain: Run multiple chains from dispersed starting points. Split R-hat compares variation within each half-chain against disagreement between halves. Splitting makes an early/late drift easier to detect. Near-one values suggest agreement in the feature compared, not convergence or coverage of every target region.

Rank-normalisation pools all split draws, assigns ranks, then converts rank fractions to standard-normal quantiles. For sorted values `[1,2,4,9]`, ranks r are `[1,2,3,4]`. With N=4 entries, the code uses $u=(r-.375)/(N+.25)$, giving approximately `[.147,.382,.618,.853]` before normal quantiles. Folding takes absolute distance from the pooled median: median 3 gives `[2,1,1,6]`. Rank those distances to expose scale disagreement. Ties receive average ranks; the code flattens entries to rank them, then reshapes ranks back into chain rows.

Report the larger rank and folded split R-hat. The code compares invented independent normal draws with a second collection whose fourth chain has twice the scale; these are diagnostic examples, not posterior traces. Also inspect traces, target knowledge and statistic-specific error. Bulk ESS (central behaviour), tail ESS and sampler-specific energy diagnostics are further-study topics, outside this calculation.
lessons.predict: Could chains have similar means yet disagree about the distribution’s scale?
lessons.look: The folded comparison exposes the deliberately changed scale. Neither collection demonstrates real MCMC exploration of a difficult posterior.
lessons.change: Shift one chain by 1 instead of changing its scale. Compare both diagnostics.
lessons.question: Four chains remain trapped in the same local mode and agree closely. What can R-hat establish?
options: That every mode has been explored.
Agreement among the sampled chains for the diagnostic, leaving missed-mode concerns unresolved.
That all draws are independent.
lessons.feedback: Agreement cannot reveal a region that none of the chains visited. Starting points, model knowledge and complementary diagnostics remain essential.
hints: Consider a second mode absent from every sample.
A comparison only has access to observed chains.
lessons.limit: This implements the rank/folded R-hat calculation, not the full modern MCMC diagnostic suite. Close-to-one R-hat is necessary evidence of agreement, not sufficient evidence of correct inference.
source: Vehtari et al. · Improved R-hat and MCMC diagnostics

lessons.title: Predict new observations
lessons.short: Propagate posterior parameter uncertainty into a future outcome distribution.
lessons.goal: Propagate posterior parameter uncertainty into a future outcome distribution.
explain: Posterior predictive sampling first draws a parameter from its posterior, then draws new observations conditional on that parameter. The resulting distribution accounts for parameter uncertainty and future outcome variability under the model. It is distinct from the posterior distribution of the parameter alone.

For the beta-binomial example, draw p from beta(20,14), then generate a future count among 20 observations with that p. Plugging the posterior mean directly into a binomial omits uncertainty in p. Both have the same expected count here, but the predictive mixture has greater variance.

The beta-binomial distribution gives an exact predictive mean and variance to check the simulation. Predictive checks compare features of replicated and observed data to reveal mismatch. A tail comparison under the fitted predictive model can be useful criticism, but does not by itself validate the prior or observation model. Keep numerical accuracy separate from model adequacy.
lessons.predict: Can the plug-in and full predictive distributions share a mean but have different spreads?
lessons.look: Count quantiles describe future group outcomes; p quantiles describe a parameter. Neither is the numerical error bar on an estimated mean.
lessons.change: Increase `future_n` to 100. Compare how parameter uncertainty contributes to the two predictive variances.
lessons.question: Which simulation represents the full posterior predictive count?
options: Fix p at its posterior mean in every draw.
Draw p from the posterior, then draw the new count conditional on that p.
Use the posterior p draw itself as the future count.
lessons.feedback: Two stages propagate both sources of variation under the model. Preserve the distinction between a parameter and an observable count.
hints: Write the units of p and of the count.
First sample the uncertain parameter, then the conditional observation.
lessons.limit: The model assumes future observations share the same p and sampling mechanism as the invented evidence. Changing conditions and model uncertainty require further analysis.

applications.title: Sizing and total cost
applications.short: Compare capacity choices and five-year cost under shared uncertain demand.
applications.goal: Compare capacity choices and five-year cost under shared uncertain demand.
explain: Sizing selects installed capacity under uncertain demand. Total cost of ownership (TCO) totals the costs inside a stated boundary; here it includes capital purchase (capex) and electricity over five years. Capacity is useful work per day. Reserve leaves headroom: the .8 factor makes only 80% of sustainable capacity available to the planned load. Prices and capacities are invented.

One small-fleet world with 8 units gives 8×220×.8=1,408 work units/day of usable capacity. Power is a rate in kilowatts (kW); energy is power times time in kilowatt-hours (kWh). At .25 kW each, 8 units use 17,520 kWh/year. At an invented £.20/kWh, five-year electricity is £17,520; adding £40,000 purchase gives £57,520. The code varies the shared world inputs, not this arithmetic.

Each world draws initial daily demand, one annual growth rate g and an energy price. Year t demand multiplies the initial value by (1+g)^t: growth compounds on earlier growth. The fleet stays fixed for five years; shortfalls are reported, not silently repaired by purchases. Costs are nominal undiscounted totals: no conversion of future payments to today's value. Staffing, support, replacements and financing require an explicit extension.
applications.predict: Should a cheaper option with insufficient capacity appear feasible merely because its mean cost is low?
applications.look: The required-unit diagnostic describes demand; it does not change the fixed fleet policy or its cost. Costs are nominal undiscounted five-year totals.
applications.change: Add a stated annual support cost per installed unit, and include it consistently for every option.
applications.question: Which comparison is meaningful before choosing a fleet?
options: Only the cheapest single simulated world.
Cost distributions together with a stated capacity reliability requirement and cost boundary.
Capital cost divided by the largest generated demand.
applications.feedback: A decision needs both a service requirement and a consistent cost boundary. Shared worlds help compare options on the same demand futures.
hints: Write the service requirement first.
A low cost is not enough when the option cannot perform the required work.
applications.limit: All prices and capacities are invented. The fixed fleet model omits failures, expansions, financing, tax, staffing and time discounting.
source: Art B. Owen · Monte Carlo theory, methods and examples
applications.notation: The code's required-unit diagnostic rounds up demand divided by usable capacity per unit; it does not buy those units during a trial. Any capacity failure means at least one of the five years fails.

applications.title: Migration deadline and budget
applications.short: Link a migration schedule to the cost of running old and new systems together.
applications.goal: Link a migration schedule to the cost of running old and new systems together.
explain: Migration couples schedule and money. Two preparation tasks run concurrently, then validation starts after both finish: duration is max(A,B)+validation. A common complexity factor can slow both tasks together. A separate idea, parallel or dual running, means operating the old and replacement services at the same time until migration completes.

This workbook charges an invented £1,800 for each day of dual running, plus a fixed transition cost. Three policies share task worlds: standard, extra staff and a smaller first release. Their supplied speed multiplier changes preparation, not validation. At 20 days the standard policy costs £15,000+20×£1,800=£51,000. These effects and prices are teaching assumptions.

Test deadline and budget jointly within each world. Their separate success fractions cannot generally be multiplied, because a longer migration costs more. A cutover switches users to the replacement; rollback returns them to the old service if that switch fails. Those events are possible extensions, not simulated here. Keep the small schedule and cost boundary inspectable before adding them.
applications.predict: If longer duration directly increases cost, can deadline and budget success be multiplied as independent events?
applications.look: The joint success indicator keeps each world’s duration and cost together. Multiplying marginal success rates would erase their connection.
applications.change: Add a £20000 rollback cost in worlds with an explicitly modelled cutover failure. State whether failure also extends duration.
applications.question: Two preparation tasks run simultaneously before validation. What is the basic finish-time rule?
options: $A+B+\mathrm{validation}$.
max(A,B)+validation.
min(A,B)+validation.
applications.feedback: Validation waits for the slower parallel branch. Summing both branches would model sequential execution instead.
hints: Draw the two parallel branches joining before validation.
The join occurs when both branches have finished.
applications.limit: Task duration and policy effects are invented. The schedule has no resource contention, calendar constraints, retries or scope-quality model.
source: Art B. Owen · Monte Carlo theory, methods and examples
applications.notation: In the illustration, T is completion time, C is cost, d is the deadline and b is the budget; $\land$ means both conditions hold and the indicator is 1 only for joint success.

applications.title: GPU job and checkpoint economics
applications.short: Account for useful work, checkpoint overhead and lost work under interruption.
applications.goal: Account for useful work, checkpoint overhead and lost work under interruption.
explain: A checkpoint saves completed progress so a job can resume there after interruption. Saving takes overhead time without advancing useful computation. Frequent saves lose less work on failure but incur more overhead. Compare policies for the same twenty hours of useful work, charging all elapsed computation and save time.

The model splits work into chunks. Suppose a 2-hour chunk fails after .6 hours, then the retry finishes in 2 hours and pays .05 hours to checkpoint: elapsed time is .6+2+.05=2.65 hours for 2 useful hours. An unsuccessful attempt loses that chunk's progress. The final successful chunk also pays overhead by convention; checkpoint saves themselves cannot be interrupted here.

Each complete-job trial uses retries until all useful chunks finish. Exponential interruption times have constant hazard, the conditional interruption rate while still computing; their supplied mean is 8 compute hours, so the hazard is 1/8 per compute hour. Shared uniform inputs match corresponding attempts across policies. Bill elapsed time at the invented hourly rate, with no restart delay and an attempt cap that fails visibly if exhausted. Real throughput, failures and pricing need evidence.
applications.predict: Will the shortest checkpoint interval always minimise billed time?
applications.look: Elapsed time includes failed attempts and successful checkpoint overhead. Useful completed work remains exactly 20 hours for every policy.
applications.change: Increase checkpoint overhead to .25 hours and predict which policy becomes less attractive.
applications.question: What must remain equal for this checkpoint-policy comparison?
options: The number of interruption events.
The required useful work and the stated billing boundary.
The number of attempted chunks.
applications.feedback: Hold the useful task fixed and account for all elapsed work and overhead. Policies can legitimately change retries and chunk counts.
hints: Separate completed useful work from repeated or checkpoint work.
The comparison concerns the cost of delivering the same useful result.
applications.limit: The model assumes constant throughput, exponential compute-only interruptions, interruption-free checkpoints, no restart delay and a flat invented price.
source: Art B. Owen · Monte Carlo theory, methods and examples
